claims.claim: Kay says he does not deliver a book until it is close to where he wants it and is therefore very lightly edited across his three English-language publishers.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Rodger Turner for SFSite

claims.claim: Kay says he likes to work with cross-sections of a culture or society and so tends to have figures from many different classes.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, quoted in Sandy Auden, 'A Question of Character', UK Sci Fi Channel website
claims.quote: cross-sections of a culture or society

claims.claim: Kay says characters he thinks of as minor grow in importance because he likes their voice.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, quoted in Sandy Auden, 'A Question of Character', UK Sci Fi Channel website
claims.quote: grow in importance because I like their voice
claims.page: early in the article, on making characters

claims.claim: Kay says telescoping the Reconquista's three hundred years into effectively two generations lets him intensify the reader's response by keeping it with one set of characters.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Guy Haley, SFX #93
claims.quote: telescoping events into effectively two generations

claims.feature: other: research must be digested not dumped
claims.claim: Kay names as failed fiction writing the book in which great gobbets of raw fact are tucked in like an undigested meal.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by James Schellenberg and David M. Switzer, Challenging Destiny #11
claims.quote: great gobbets of raw fact are tucked into the book
claims.page: answer on balancing nonfiction and fiction

claims.feature: other: history as residue on ordinary lives
claims.claim: Kay says that in Sailing to Sarantium he wanted the protagonist to be less central to the great events and to examine how those great events impact ordinary lives.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, chat transcript, Event Horizon 'Flashpoint' hosted by Jim Freund
claims.quote: how those great events can impact on ordinary lives
claims.page: early in the transcript, on the premise

claims.feature: other: worldbuilding consistency as a game
claims.claim: Kay says Tolkien would have constructed an elaborate explanation for a map discrepancy as part of his worldbuilding game, and declines to do so himself.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, chat transcript, Event Horizon
claims.page: answer to Ran on the maps in Lions and Sarantium

claims.feature: other: know the period before varying it
claims.claim: Kay says that a fantasy based on a period is a variation on a theme and that a writer has to know the theme before trying variations.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed for Deep Magic ezine
claims.quote: you have to KNOW the theme before you try variations

claims.feature: other: intuition described after the fact
claims.claim: Kay warns readers to be sceptical when writers present intuitive processes as thought-out planning, saying his own approach was an evolution he discovered rather than a strategy laid out in advance.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History', boingboing.net
claims.quote: be skeptical when writers present intuitive processes as thought-out planning

claims.feature: other: no dates or facts on the page
claims.claim: Kay names as a risk of his method that readers will never learn the year of the Treaty of Utrecht in his novels and will not have a desire to learn the real facts assuaged.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History', boingboing.net
claims.quote: Readers will never learn the year of the Treaty of Utrecht

claims.claim: Kay says that in The Lions of Al-Rassan he wanted to explore interactions not ideologies.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History', boingboing.net
claims.quote: I wanted to explore interactions not ideologies

claims.feature: other: the reader completes the book
claims.claim: Kay says each reader makes the book they read.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History', boingboing.net
claims.quote: each reader makes the book they read
claims.page: body, A Song for Arbonne section

claims.claim: Kay says his main contribution to the discussion of writing advice is that there are no rules.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Some Writing Advice: Don't Take Others' Advice', LitHub

claims.claim: Kay cites, as an instance of the writing-advice industry he is allergic to, that people everywhere tell you not to use italics.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Some Writing Advice', LitHub
claims.quote: People everywhere tell you not to use italics

claims.feature: other: the past rhymes rather than repeats
claims.claim: Kay says he writes with the idea that history may not repeat but it rhymes, attributing the line to the psychoanalyst Theodore Reik rather than Mark Twain.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The Big Idea', Whatever (John Scalzi's blog)
claims.quote: history may not repeat, but it rhymes
claims.page: body, on Written on the Dark
